pair_convention.spot_explanation: GBP/JPY at 210.72084 means 1 GBP = 210.72084 JPY. Rising = sterling strengthening against the yen. Falling = sterling weakening against the yen, equivalently the yen strengthening against sterling. Sterling is the high-yielding leg at a 275bp policy advantage, so this is a classic G10 carry cross: a long position is paid to hold and a short position pays roughly 282.9bp annualised on the store's futures-implied roll premium.

executive_summary: GBP/JPY trades at 210.72084 (the gated store's 3 September close, two sessions after the 1 September valuation date), having fallen 0.84% over one month, 1.38% over three and 1.20% over six while remaining 5.43% higher over twelve — a pair whose twelve-month carry-driven ascent has stalled and begun to reverse. The dominant bilateral narrative is the simultaneous repricing of a 275bp policy differential from both ends: the Bank of England holds at 3.75% with roughly +7bp priced for 17 September, and the Bank of Japan meets the following day with 80-90% of a hike to 1.25% discounted, so Japan speaks last and the differential can close to 250bp inside twenty-four hours with no scheduled UK reply until 5 November. The chart arriving after the direction verdict was scored corroborates it rather than contradicts it: a 580-pip two-session collapse on 2-3 September, attributed in market reporting to a Tokyo rate check and hawkish BoJ repricing, has left spot below the 50-day (216.01), 100-day (215.05) and 200-day (213.04) simple moving averages while those three remain in a rising stack — the signature of a fresh breakdown rather than a mature downtrend. Three bilateral differentials diverge materially from the standalone dossiers: the energy shock that damages sterling in the GBP dossier and the yen in the JPY dossier nets pair-positive, because Japan is the double-negative on both crude and LNG while sterling takes a single negative on gas; the two sovereigns' fiscal premia largely cancel, so Factor 8 trades the difference in credibility rather than the level of yields; and bilateral goods trade of roughly USD 18bn two-way is immaterial, so there is no structural flow anchor in either direction. The settled verdict is Bearish at conviction 2 tactically and Bearish at conviction 3 strategically, and our reading of the price payload is that it argues for holding those convictions rather than raising them. The caveat is carry and structure in combination: a short pays 282.9bp annualised — 46 pips over four weeks and 299 pips over six months — and below the thin 2-touch shelf at 208.35-210.07 the chart is structurally unmapped until 203.45, so the distribution is a slow bleed punctuated by air-pocket gaps rather than an orderly trend.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no pair-level PPP source in the free stack, and none is asserted. The only trade-weighted comparison available is the BIS real effective exchange rate, where sterling sits at 111.41 for June 2026 — the third-highest in the G10+SGD set — against a yen at 65.3, the cheapest major currency in the world and 30.4 points below the next cheapest. Both dossiers independently translate that 46-point gap into a REER-parity implied cross of GBP/JPY 127.03, which places spot at 210.72084 roughly 66% above the level that would equalise the two real exchange rates. That is a genuine structural misalignment and it is the single largest number in this report, but it carries no timing information whatsoever: the yen has been this cheap for three years and got 8.73 points cheaper in the year to June while sterling barely moved. The correct use of the valuation signal here is as a magnitude constraint on the bullish case rather than a driver of the bearish one — it bounds how much further the pair can extend before an official sector that has already spent roughly JPY 27.1trn in a calendar year objects, and it says nothing about the next four weeks. What is priced in the current level is a 275bp differential assumed to persist, funded at a cross-currency basis of roughly -7.9bp, with the forward curve discounting the pair 282.9bp annualised purely through covered interest parity rather than through any forecast.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since late July has been one of a carry trade that keeps re-forming and keeps being knocked over by official flow. The 30-31 July joint Japan-US intervention took the pair from a 218.49715 close on 29 July to 211.17739 by 3 August, roughly 730 pips in three sessions; leveraged funds then rebuilt 23,972 contracts of yen short over three weeks and the pair recovered to 217.30522 by 25 August, more than 80% of the loss. That recovery was erased in two days at the start of September, with the cross dropping more than 300 pips on speculation of intervention driven by a Tokyo rate check, and the yen reaching a one-month intraday high on 3 September. The transmission mechanism into this cross is well established: when Japanese intervention is anticipated, a large share of transactions passes through cross pairs such as EUR/JPY and GBP/JPY, and pricing distortions often appear in the crosses before the headline dollar-yen rate moves. The pair is therefore not merely a passenger in the yen story — it is one of the vehicles.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The policy differential is +275bp: Bank Rate at 3.75% as of 2026-08-28 against the Bank of Japan's target of around 1.00% as of 2026-09-01. The sovereign 10-year differential in the payload is +212.6bp but is built from two monthly observations both dated 2026-06-01 and roughly 92 days stale; on live prints the ten-year gap is nearer 216bp and compressing because the Japanese leg is rising while the gilt is not. What a position actually pays is the store's futures-implied roll premium of -282.9bp annualised, observed 2026-08-31, which by covered interest parity equals the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis — a 7.9bp wedge against the 275bp policy differential that is basis, not rate, meaning a long earns marginally more than pure policy carry and a short pays marginally more than the differential. Carry-to-volatility depends entirely on the denominator accepted: 0.341 against 60-day realised (8.07%), 0.371 against the 3-month implied estimate (7.419%), 0.324 against a bias-corrected implied (~8.5%) — a band of roughly 0.32 to 0.37 that has deteriorated over the last fortnight purely because realised volatility rose from 8.07% to 8.75%, not because the differential moved. The carry regime is still working in the sense that the environment rewards it — VIX near its 2026 low, tight credit spreads, equities at records — but it has stopped paying on this specific cross: over the six months to 3 September the pair lost 1.20% of spot while paying roughly 1.41% of carry to a long holder, for a total return of approximately +0.21%. The four-week carry cost of a bearish expression (46 pips) is immaterial relative to a 120-pip ATR, while the six-month cost (299 pips) consumes more than a third of the base-case strategic move, which is why spot is favoured tactically and optionality strategically.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Bank Rate at 3.75% against the BoJ's 1.00% target gives sterling a 275bp policy advantage, the payload's policyDifferential of 2.75, and the second-widest gap sterling owns after the franc. The level is not the question; the direction of travel over four weeks is, and it points one way. The Bank of England decides on 17 September with only about +7bp priced and 56 of 64 economists in a mid-August Reuters poll expecting no change for the rest of 2026, while the Bank of Japan decides on 18 September with roughly 80-90% of a 25bp move to 1.25% priced. The sequencing matters twice over: Japan speaks last, and if it delivers while the MPC holds, the differential closes from 275bp to 250bp inside twenty-four hours with no offsetting UK move available until 5 November. The long end says the same thing more slowly: the payload's 10-year differential of 212.6bp is built from two stale June monthly observations, and on live prints the gilt at 5.16% against a JGB that touched 3.00% on 1 September leaves roughly 216bp, compressing because the Japanese leg is rising while the gilt is not. Transmission is direct and mechanical — this cross is a carry vehicle, and the carry is the thesis, so a narrowing differential reduces the compensation for holding the position at the same time as it reduces the fundamental case for it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential compresses from both ends and neither leg has a credible path to widening it. The Bank of Japan is expected by 35 of 54 economists to reach at least 1.50% by end-March 2027, with half of 36 respondents naming 1.75% as terminal and 36% naming 2.00% or higher, and the schedule gives it three chances inside the window on 18 September, 30 October with an Outlook Report and 18 December. The Bank of England, by contrast, holds a genuinely symmetric reaction function whose resolution the Committee itself has tied to 2027 pay settlements arriving "towards the end of this year" — that is, at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report and the 17 December decision — with private-sector regular pay already at 2.8% against a target-consistent estimate of about 3.25% and unemployment at 4.9% and rising. On the central paths the 275bp gap becomes roughly 200-225bp by the first quarter of 2027, and the tail risks are asymmetric: a BoJ overshoot to 2.00% and a BoE cut both narrow it further, while the only widening scenario requires the BoE's three standing hawks to win a fourth vote at the November forecast round. The 30 October Outlook Report is the highest-stakes dated event for the pair because it is a full projection round at which the FY2027 core CPI forecast, already revised up to 2.4%, is remarked, and it lands six days before the MPR. Transmission is the same carry channel, but over six months the level of compensation matters as much as its direction: a 283bp roll premium shrinking toward 200bp removes roughly a third of the reason to own the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is roughly 1.0 percentage point in sterling's favour on headline (UK 2.9% versus Japan 1.9%) and 0.8 points on core (2.6% versus 1.8%), but both are converging and the convergence is what the pair trades. UK services CPI, the BoE's own underlying gauge, fell to 3.4% from 3.6% and input PPI missed hard at 4.9% against 6.6% expected, while Japanese core has risen three consecutive months in the Tokyo series and the BoJ's own measure excluding fresh food and institutional factors is 2.3%, above target for twenty-two months, with the July Outlook expecting core "clearly above 2 percent from the second half of fiscal 2026" as energy subsidies unwind. On growth the UK is still nominally ahead at 1.2% year-on-year against Japan's 0.55%, but the momentum runs the other way: UK unemployment is 4.9% and rising with payrolled employees down 210,000 on the year, against Japanese unemployment falling to 2.4% with a jobs-to-applicants ratio of 1.18 and a third consecutive shunto above 5%. Asymmetric sensitivity is the transmission: Japanese data moves this cross harder than UK data right now because the BoJ path is live and repricing while the BoE is priced as static, so a Japanese CPI beat converts directly into differential compression whereas a UK CPI beat runs into a committee that has said it is on hold. The two prints land on consecutive days, UK CPI on 16 September and Japanese national CPI on 17 September, immediately before both decisions.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Extend the horizon and the labour markets decide it, because they are the slowest-moving and most reliable series on either side and they point in opposite directions. The UK has a loosening market — 4.9% unemployment up 0.2 points on the year, vacancies at 705,000 and the lowest since early 2021, private-sector regular pay at 2.8% against a target-consistent 3.25% and real regular pay growth of only 0.5% — which is the configuration in which an energy-driven headline CPI erodes real income rather than feeding wages. Japan has the mirror image: 2.4% unemployment, a third consecutive shunto above 5%, real wages positive for six months and nominal earnings above 3% for five, the longest such run in 34 years, with corporate one-year inflation expectations at 2.7% and output-price diffusion at +40. The inflation differential therefore compresses structurally rather than cyclically, and with it the justification for a 275bp policy gap. The honest counterweight is breadth: Japan's weighted median CPI is only 1.1% and services inflation 1.2%, so the Japanese regime is narrower than the headline suggests and a queued rice disinflation is visible, while the UK's five-year record of above-target inflation means the BoE cannot cut quickly. That caps confidence at 58 rather than higher, but it does not change the sign — an economy with a tightening labour market and a hiking central bank against one with a loosening labour market and a static central bank is a bearish configuration for the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest pair-positive factor and it is the reason the tactical verdict is a lean rather than a call. Risk appetite is as supportive of a carry cross as it has been all year: VIX closed 14.51 on 27 August, down 3.70 points on the month and near the 2026 low of 14.13; US investment grade spreads are 79bp and high yield 263bp, the latter 21bp tighter on the month; the S&P 500 is at records with a 13.1% year-to-date total return and the Nikkei is up 58.4% over twelve months. The bilateral asymmetry is that sterling is mildly risk-positive while the yen is the G10's strongest negative-beta currency to volatility, so the same benign regime pushes both legs in the pair-positive direction and the effects compound rather than cancel. Transmission is the carry channel itself: with realised volatility on the cross at 7.06% against a 275bp differential, the risk-adjusted attraction of a long position is roughly 0.37-0.39, which is precisely the configuration in which leveraged funds add. The offsets are real but they are about room rather than direction. At 14.51 VIX and 79bp investment grade there is essentially no risk premium left to compress, so this factor is a tailwind of diminishing size; and the tail is live, with US and Iranian forces exchanging fire on 30-31 August and a US appropriations deadline on 30 September. Over four weeks the observable state dominates and the observable state is pair-positive.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor stops carrying direction for this pair and becomes a variance amplifier, which is why the stance is Neutral at the default 0.05 weight. The modal path is persistence: if VIX stays near 14 and credit stays near 79bp, the carry keeps working and the pair keeps grinding higher for another six months exactly as it has. That is why the stance is not Bearish. But the starting conditions can only deteriorate, and every deterioration scenario is pair-negative and unusually violent for this cross specifically, because GBP/JPY combines a currency exposed to a dated domestic fiscal event with the currency that receives the entire proceeds of a global carry unwind. The named ingredients are identifiable: a US labour market that printed -23,000 payrolls in July with 103,000 of downward revisions while the Fed hikes into it, a 30 September appropriations deadline in a year that has already seen two shutdowns, US midterms on 3 November, and an unresolved Hormuz situation. Both dossiers also record the yen-cross skew already pricing this — the USD/JPY one-month 25-delta risk reversal is -1.74 volatility points and EUR/JPY is more negative still at -1.84, telling you the option market is paying heavily for yen upside on the crosses. Because the high-probability path is pair-positive and the lower-probability path is violently pair-negative, and because six months gives the tail time to occur, Neutral is the honest label rather than a compromise.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the structural flows dominate the futures data and they are pair-negative on both legs. On the yen side, Japanese life-insurer currency hedge ratios are at historically low levels — corroborated independently by Daiwa's April 2026 survey of ten majors and by a Bank of Japan Review — and Daiwa states the consequence explicitly: raising them would prompt a corresponding demand to purchase yen. The trigger is a normal consequence of the base-case rate path rather than a shock, because hedging costs fall as the BoJ hikes and the Fed's cutting cycle resumes. Alongside it, Japanese residents sold a net JPY 1,978.4bn of foreign bonds and JPY 869.0bn of foreign equities in the week 16-22 August, a JPY 5.5trn week-on-week swing, and GPIF ended June with foreign equities at 25.33% against a 25.0% policy target, mechanically implying multi-trillion-yen foreign asset sales. On the sterling side the structural channel points the same way: overseas investors hold 25-30% of outstanding gilts and UK pension and insurance funds adjust foreign-asset hedge ratios dynamically — the LDI mechanism that turned the 2022 gilt crisis into a sterling crisis — and the 28 October Budget is live. Neither channel is measurable weekly, which is why confidence is 54, but both point in the same direction and both would express themselves through this cross rather than around it.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral tactically and Bearish strategically because the two datasets run on different clocks. Over four weeks the observable CFTC positions on both legs are mid-distribution and generate no signal. Over one to six months the binding flows are Japanese lifer and GPIF rebalancing on one side and UK institutional hedge ratios on the other, both of which can only move in the pair-negative direction from their current starting points, and both of which are triggered by the base-case rate path rather than by a shock.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Short both legs at the headline, so the net pair signal is muted; but leveraged funds are long GBP 40,670 and short JPY 77,042, a fast-money long GBP/JPY held on both legs simultaneously. There is no crowded pair-short to squeeze.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A Japanese national core CPI print at or above 2.0% on 17 September followed by a BoJ hike on 18 September delivered with explicit acceleration language, against a BoE that holds on 17 September with the vote split softening from 6-3 to 7-2 — that sequence reprices both legs of the differential inside 48 hours while the reactive money is positioned the wrong way.
tactical.historical_analogue: The 31 July-3 August episode: a record joint MoF and US Treasury yen-buying operation forced 41,165 contracts of yen short-covering in a single week and moved USD/JPY roughly nine big figures, with the yen crosses carried along; it retraced more than half within four weeks, which is why the analogue argues for a spike rather than a trend.
tactical.contrarian_case: The market has now watched the yen fail to hold a record intervention, fail to rally through a 30-year high in JGB yields and fail to respond to a narrowing UST-JGB spread — three yen-positive impulses that produced net yen depreciation — and has correctly concluded that yen rallies are for selling. On that reading, a 275bp carry cross with a 30th-percentile sterling short still to cover and a benign risk regime is a buy on any dip, and both September decisions are already priced so there is no fresh catalyst to sell into.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: Structurally pair-negative on both legs — Japanese lifer hedge ratios at record lows and GPIF above its foreign-equity target on one side, UK dynamic hedgers and 25-30% foreign gilt ownership on the other. The visible futures shorts are small; the invisible pair-negative flow capacity is measured in trillions of yen.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A UK Budget on 28 October that fails to satisfy the fiscal rules credibly, forcing liquidation of the leveraged sterling long on top of fresh shorting, coinciding with a BoJ Outlook Report on 30 October that revises core CPI up again — the two events fall two days apart, the specific clustering risk in this pair.
strategic.historical_analogue: Two analogues apply, one per leg: September 2022, when sterling fell roughly 8% against the dollar in the fortnight around the mini-Budget precisely because the market was not short going in; and August 2024, when a yen carry unwind moved the yen crosses violently from a positioning base more extreme than today's, which cuts both ways since today's readings have room to build first.
strategic.contrarian_case: A genuine strategic contrarian case for the pair exists and rests on three legs. The BoE retains three standing hawks who vote again at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report, so a fourth vote would restore the differential rather than close it. Japan's own fiscal arithmetic means a hiking BoJ raises the debt-service line by roughly JPY 5trn per 100bp against a request that already assumes 3.8%, so part of the JGB yield rise is risk premium with no yen-positive content — precisely why the yen has not rallied on rising Japanese yields. And a durable Hormuz reopening would relieve the UK energy import bill while leaving Bank Rate at 3.75%, the most pair-positive combination available. We hold the bearish stance but size strategic conviction at 3 rather than 4 for exactly these reasons.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor where the two legs are hit by the same shock, and the netting genuinely favours the pair rising. Both economies are net energy importers facing a severely disrupted Strait of Hormuz, but Japan is the more exposed in gross terms: it imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons, mineral fuels were 22.1% of July imports and rose 53.5% year on year on falling volumes, its terms-of-trade index has collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 to 81.62 in July and June produced its first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months. The UK's shock is real but narrower — NBP gas at 161-165 pence per therm against the BoE's own 136-pence July conditioning assumption, with some domestic production and a crude leg that has actually improved as Brent fell from its July peak. The framework's own direction rules make the netting explicit: oil up is a double negative for the yen and a single negative for sterling, LNG up is a double negative for the yen, and NBP gas up is a single negative for sterling. So an escalating energy shock hurts the yen more, and the pair rises. Bilateral trade is immaterial and worth stating plainly: IMF DOTS 2024 shows UK exports to Japan of USD 9.3bn against imports of USD 8.6bn for a net UK surplus of USD 0.7bn, roughly USD 18bn of two-way goods trade, which is a rounding error against this cross's turnover and creates no structural flow driver in either direction.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At the framework's heaviest non-policy strategic weight of 0.16 this factor contributes nothing, and that is a finding rather than a dodge: the two legs offset almost exactly, on opposite measures. On levels Japan is unambiguously the stronger external position — a current account of +5.04% of GDP and a record first-half surplus of JPY 17.43trn against the UK's -2.84% of GDP, a 7.9 percentage point gap, and it is the UK that must sell its currency to fund a 7.6%-of-GDP goods deficit whose offsetting services surplus actually FELL by GBP 1.2bn in the same quarter. On the margin Japan is deteriorating faster and from a more fragile composition — its surplus is primary income at 27.6 times the goods surplus, which is a stock return that does not generate spot flow the way trade does, while the goods account that does generate flow has turned negative; Japan has slipped to third-largest net creditor behind Germany and China, and the yen's share of allocated global reserves fell 0.40 points to 5.44% in Q1. Layer on the framework's commodity rules, which say the same shock costs the yen more, and the heating season falling inside the window with Hormuz unresolved, and the two readings genuinely cancel: level says short the pair, flow and commodity netting say own it. Neutral at 50 is the honest output, and it mechanically caps the strategic score by neutralising 16% of the weight.

Both errors are real and they point in opposite directions for this cross, which is why we decline a directional stance at a 0.16 weight rather than manufacture one.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish tactically at 50 and Neutral strategically at 50, on the same evidence read at different distances. Over four weeks what matters is the marginal energy headline, and by the framework's own direction rules that hurts the yen more than sterling because Japan imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons — so the pair rises. Over one to six months the level of the external position re-enters, and Japan's +5.04% of GDP against the UK's -2.84% offsets the flow and commodity netting almost exactly. The weight change from 0.06 to 0.16 makes that offset the single largest mechanical difference between the two horizons.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: Net energy importer running a 2.84%-of-GDP current account deficit. Direct exposure is UK NBP natural gas at 161-165 pence per therm in the last week of August, roughly 18-21% above the Bank of England's own 136-pence July conditioning assumption and about 43% higher year-on-year, plus a crude import bill that improved as Brent fell 12% from its July peak. Some domestic North Sea production partially offsets. Framework sign: oil up = -GBP (mild); NBP gas up = -GBP.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: The most energy-dependent currency in the G10 set, importing essentially all of its oil and the large majority of its gas. July mineral fuel imports were JPY 2,680.4bn, 22.1% of all imports and up 53.5% year on year, with crude value +87.8% on volume +5.5%, LNG value +22.5% on volume -4.8% and coal value +33.4% on volume -5.5% — price, not demand. JKM LNG is up 101.9% year on year. Framework sign: oil up = --JPY; LNG (JKM) up = --JPY.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Step one, apply the direction rules to each leg. Oil up: sterling takes a single negative, the yen a double negative. LNG and JKM up: the yen takes a double negative, sterling no direct hit. NBP gas up: sterling takes a single negative, the yen no direct hit. Step two, net across the basket actually moving. Crude and LNG are both elevated with Hormuz disrupted, and both are yen-double-negatives, while only NBP gas is a sterling-specific negative and the sterling crude leg has improved. Step three, translate into pair direction. Because GBP is the base and JPY the quote, a shock that damages the quote currency more pushes GBP/JPY UP. Step four, sanity-check against the observable series: Japan's terms of trade fell 9.8% in two quarters to 81.62 while the UK's deterioration is concentrated in a single commodity running 18-21% above a policy assumption. Conclusion: a common energy shock is pair-POSITIVE, and a genuine energy relief is pair-NEGATIVE. This is the single most counterintuitive result in the analysis, because it means the factor that most damages sterling in its own dossier and most damages the yen in its own dossier is, bilaterally, a mild positive for GBP/JPY.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Brent from roughly USD 90-93 to USD 100-102: yen takes a double negative through crude and, via correlated JKM, a second LNG hit; sterling takes a single negative on crude plus a probable NBP sympathy move. Net pair impact is positive but modest — perhaps a third of the yen's damage offset by sterling's — and it would be amplified by the simultaneous risk-off impulse only if the shock were disorderly enough to trigger a carry unwind, which would reverse the sign entirely. That path dependency is why confidence here is only 50.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent to roughly USD 81-84 on a credible Hormuz reopening: Japan's terms of trade recover from 81.62 toward the mid-80s and the goods account improves fastest because its deterioration was almost entirely price rather than volume; the UK also benefits, and the dossiers name a durable reopening as the single most sterling-positive event available because it would collapse the energy bill while leaving Bank Rate at 3.75%. On the direction rules the yen gains more, so the net pair impact is negative — energy relief is pair-bearish. Both dossiers assess a durable reopening at roughly 20% probability.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: LNG, specifically the JKM-NBP complex, is the dominant driver for this pair rather than crude. JKM is up 101.9% year on year and is a double negative for the yen; NBP is 18-21% above the BoE's conditioning assumption and a single negative for sterling; and roughly one-fifth of global LNG trade normally transits the Strait of Hormuz, so the two prices now share a single supply choke point. The bilateral question is which of two importers is hurt more by the same molecule, and on gross dependence it is Japan.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance divergence is as clean as this framework ever gets: one central bank is signalling that it will tighten faster than the market expects and the other is signalling that it might do either. The Bank of Japan's 10 August Summary of Opinions contains the lines that "the pace of policy interest rate hikes will be faster than market expectations" and that it is "necessary for the Bank to accelerate the pace of adjustment"; the July Outlook calls CPI risks "skewed to the upside"; Takata dissented FOR a move to 1.25% on 31 July — a hawkish dissent, the mirror image of June's dovish one; Ueda said currency volatility's impact on inflation "may be becoming bigger than in the past"; and Himino, in the last scheduled communication before the meeting, called for raising rates "in a timely manner" and said a weak yen could push up inflation faster than in the past. Against that the BoE's 29 July minutes are the most explicitly two-sided of the cycle: a 6-3 hold, three hawks at 4.00%, Taylor describing an economy "drifting further toward deficient demand", and Ramsden explicitly two-way. Sequencing amplifies the divergence, because the BoE speaks on 17 September and the BoJ on 18 September, so Japan sets the tone and the UK has no scheduled reply until 5 November. The offset that caps confidence is a credibility differential running the other way: the market has repeatedly discounted yen-positive guidance, which is why 80-90% of a hike coexists with only one hike priced to year-end.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance channel is the second-heaviest weight at 0.12 and the divergence is durable rather than tactical. The BoJ has changed its stated objective — the July Outlook replaced lifting inflation toward 2% with stabilising it and preventing an upward deviation, which mechanically converts every upside inflation surprise from a reason to celebrate into a reason to tighten — revised FY2027 core CPI UP to 2.4% while attributing the FY2026 cut to temporary energy subsidies, and abolished scheduled interim assessments of its bond-purchase plan so that balance-sheet changes now happen ad hoc at meetings, raising the probability of an unscheduled hawkish surprise. The BoE has done the opposite: it has published a genuinely symmetric reaction function, named 2027 pay settlements as the decisive unresolved input, and told the market it expects to learn about them "towards the end of this year", which places the resolution at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report and the 17 December decision. On the incoming evidence — private-sector pay at 2.8%, DMP year-ahead wage expectations at 3.4% and falling, three-year CPI expectations at 2.8% — that resolution leans dovish. So the strategic configuration is a bank with directional guidance and rising forecasts against a bank with symmetric guidance and softening inputs, and the 30 October Outlook Report precedes the 5 November MPR by six days, so Japan again frames the comparison.

Our strategic edge is that the discount exists because the market has twice been taught this year that yen-positive news does not stick — a lesson that has a dated expiry, at the 30 October Outlook Report and the 18 December decision.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons Bearish with strategic confidence of 62 above tactical 58, and the weight nearly doubling from 0.07 to 0.12. Guidance operates on expectations, which reprice over months rather than weeks. Tactically the divergence is real but the BoE side is already fully aligned with pricing and the BoJ side is 80-90% discounted for September, so only the press-conference language is in play. Strategically the reframed BoJ objective, the upward-revised FY2027 forecast and the abolition of scheduled balance-sheet assessments compound into a reaction function that is systematically more hawkish than the market's own terminal assumption, against a BoE whose incoming wage evidence leans the other way.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The tactical event distribution is asymmetric in the pair-negative direction for one specific reason: official flow in the yen only ever goes one way. Japan bought roughly JPY 27.1trn of yen in calendar 2026, including JPY 15,399.3bn between 30 July and 26 August and a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July, the Finance Minister has said Japan "will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention", and the US Treasury Secretary repeated the commitment at the G20 on 31 August. Suspected intervention on 2 September spilled across the yen crosses. There is therefore a well-capitalised, publicly committed official bid for the yen and no corresponding official seller, and that bid transmits to GBP/JPY because this cross is a standard vehicle for expressing yen shorts. On the sterling side the four-week calendar is dense but non-binary — scheduled releases with published consensus, and the political transition to Prime Minister Burnham and Chancellor Healey has been absorbed with the Budget date fixed. The genuine binaries are the two adjacent decisions themselves. The offset is that the demonstrated half-life of intervention in this complex is under a month.

The one-way nature of official yen flow is the part that is structurally under-priced.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both legs acquire dated fiscal-political binaries, and the sterling one is both earlier and less priced. The UK Autumn Budget on 28 October arrives with an OBR forecast, a Chancellor appointed three weeks before the date was set under a Prime Minister who took office on 20 July, an OBR March headroom figure of GBP 9.9bn that a 39bp year-on-year rise in the 10-year gilt has plausibly consumed at roughly GBP 2.5bn of debt service per 0.25 points, and a 30-year gilt entrenched within 5bp of its May 2026 multi-decade peak. The distribution around it is skewed pair-negative because the fiscal rules cap the good outcome while the gilt market punishes the bad one. Japan's equivalent is the FY2027 draft budget in late December — ministry requests of about JPY 143trn with a record JPY 36.6trn debt-service line at a 3.8% assumed rate — which is pair-POSITIVE if it disappoints, since a Japanese fiscal risk premium weakens the yen. The two therefore partially offset, but the UK event lands two days before the 30 October BoJ Outlook Report, so the cluster in late October is one-sided against the pair while Japan's arrives at the very edge of the window. Add the continuing one-way official yen bid and the unresolved Hormuz situation, which by Factor 5's netting hurts the yen more, and the net is a modest bearish tilt rather than a strong one.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons Bearish, with strategic confidence of 56 above tactical 54 for different reasons rather than a stronger version of the same one. Tactically the asymmetry is official flow — a publicly committed, bilateral yen bid with no counterpart — against a UK calendar of scheduled releases. Strategically the asymmetry is the 28 October Budget, a genuine binary whose payoff is skewed by fiscal rules capping the upside and a multi-decade-high long gilt amplifying the downside, partially offset by Japan's own late-December fiscal event which would be pair-positive.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Raised tactically from 0.04 to 0.05 and strategically from 0.07 to 0.09. For most pairs this is a background factor; GBP/JPY is the rare cross where BOTH legs have acute long-end sovereign stress simultaneously — a gilt-Bund spread at 184bp, the widest since the 2022 mini-Budget, against a 10-year JGB at 3.00% for the first time since 1996 with an inverted 25s30s — and both have dated fiscal events inside the strategic horizon. Netting two live fiscal premia is genuinely material to this pair rather than boilerplate.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both sovereigns are under pressure at the long end and the netting is close, which is why confidence is only 52 despite two strong individual cases. The UK's 10-year gilt closed 5.16% on 28 August, the highest since May 2026 and 19bp higher on the month, with the 30-year at 5.73-5.76% and a gilt-Bund spread of about 184bp — a premium being paid on the debt of a country whose central bank is less likely to hike than the ECB, which is a sovereign risk premium rather than a rate-expectations premium. Japan's 10-year touched 3.00% on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 2-year hit a 31-year high of 1.743%, the 5-year set a record and the 25s30s spread is INVERTED at -1.0bp, which is the signature of concentrated duration supply meeting a buyer base that has stopped extending. Crucially both legs share the same perverse transmission: a yield rise driven by fiscal premium rather than policy expectation weakens rather than strengthens the currency, and both dossiers document it — the UK's cable-to-30-year correlation flips negative in a crisis, and the yen's failure to rally through a 30-year high in JGB yields is direct evidence of the same mechanism. The bearish tilt for the pair comes from the differences: 25-30% of gilts are foreign-held against roughly 90% domestic ownership of JGBs, the BoJ still buys JPY 2.5trn a month while the BoE runs down a GBP 491bn book, and the UK's premium has a dated resolution on 28 October while Japan's does not until late December.

Tactically the two premia largely offset — which is the finding — with the pair-negative tilt coming from foreign gilt ownership, the absence of a UK central bank buyer and the fact that the UK's premium has a dated resolution six weeks out while Japan's does not.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two fiscal stories diverge in resolution rather than in severity. Japan's arithmetic is worse in absolute terms — gross debt above 200% of GDP on the IMF-style measure, a debt-service request of JPY 36.6trn at a 3.8% assumed rate that rose by roughly JPY 5trn when the assumption moved 80bp, and a widening deficit path — but it carries three stable Big Three ratings with no action in 2026, roughly 90% domestic ownership, and a central bank that is still the largest buyer. That combination makes a disorderly Japanese outcome a tail rather than a base case, and it also means a Japanese fiscal accident is pair-POSITIVE because it weakens the yen. The UK's is smaller in stock but sharper in resolution: net debt 95.1% of GDP, the OBR's March GBP 9.9bn of headroom plausibly consumed, three options for Chancellor Healey on 28 October of which the third — changing the rules — is the one the gilt market will not tolerate, ratings at AA and AA- with Moody's variously reported and no 2026 action so the downgrade risk lies ahead, and GBP 246.2bn of gross gilt sales to be absorbed while the BoE runs its own book down. The netting therefore favours the pair falling: the sovereign with the dated catalyst, the foreign ownership, the rating vulnerability and no central bank buyer is the base currency.

The honest summary is that the fundamental differential is closing while the market environment still pays handsomely to ignore that. tactical.rationale: At the applied tactical weights, Policy & Rates at 0.24 and Inflation & Growth at 0.18 carry 42% of the score and both are pair-negative, contributing -0.2256 of the -0.3192 gross negative — so this is a relative-policy-path call with a data overlay, and if the Japanese policy and inflation channel disappoints the score collapses toward neutral. The dominant mechanism is dated and mechanical: sterling earns 275bp over the yen, the Bank of England decides on 17 September with about +7bp priced and 56 of 64 economists expecting no change all year, and the Bank of Japan decides the following day with roughly 80-90% of a 25bp move to 1.25% priced. Japan speaks last, and if it delivers while the MPC holds, the differential closes to 250bp inside twenty-four hours with no scheduled UK reply until 5 November. Guidance reinforces this rather than duplicating it: the BoJ's 10 August Summary of Opinions says the pace of hikes will be faster than market expectations while the BoE's July minutes are the most explicitly two-sided of its cycle, with Ramsden two-way and Taylor citing deficient demand. The two standalone dossiers reinforce rather than conflict — GBP tactical Bearish at -0.1456 and JPY tactical Bullish at +0.1270, which is pair-negative on both legs — and that agreement is why the verdict is not Neutral despite modest per-factor confidence. Three bilateral facts modify the standalone views materially, and two of them cut the other way. First, bilateral trade is immaterial: IMF DOTS 2024 shows USD 9.3bn of UK exports to Japan against USD 8.6bn of imports for a net USD 0.7bn, so there is no structural flow channel and Factor 5 becomes purely a commodity-netting question. Second, that netting is pair-POSITIVE, because both legs are energy importers and the framework's own direction rules make the yen the double-negative on both oil and LNG while sterling takes a single negative on gas — the shock that damages sterling in its own dossier damages the yen more. Third, both sovereigns have simultaneous long-end fiscal stress, a gilt-Bund spread at 184bp against a 10-year JGB at 3.00%, which largely cancels and leaves only the ownership and central-bank-buyer asymmetry. What is priced is both September decisions; what is not is the BoJ terminal, with the market implying only about 1.21% after 18 December against an economist consensus of 1.75%, and a BoE whose next move is more likely a cut than the hike the curve has pushed to 2027. The path of least resistance is modestly lower into the 16-18 September cluster, where UK CPI, Japanese CPI and the two decisions land in three days, and then contested. Dated catalysts: 3 September 30-year JGB auction, 4 September US payrolls, 8 September Japanese GDP revision and balance of payments, 15 September UK labour market, 16 September UK CPI and the FOMC, 17 September BoE plus Japanese national CPI, 18 September BoJ, 30 September Japanese interim fiscal half-year end and the US appropriations deadline. Conviction is 2 rather than 3 for three specific reasons: a short position pays roughly 283bp annualised to be held, both September decisions are already discounted so the edge is in language rather than outcome, and the pair has repeatedly refused to price yen-positive news — a record joint intervention, a 30-year high in JGB yields and a narrowing UST-JGB spread together produced net yen depreciation in August. Direction, not size, is what this score supports.

Among yen-cross shorts it ranks first on fundamentals — sterling is the weakest quote-side leg available — but second on execution behind short CHF/JPY, the only long-yen expression in the G10 that is paid to wait at +100bp of policy carry with both legs safe havens. GBP/JPY is the right fundamental view expressed through the most expensive available instrument: 275bp of adverse carry and, on the payload's own numbers, the highest realised volatility of the sterling complex at 8.07% on a 60-day basis.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the pair thesis becomes broad-based rather than a single-factor call. Policy & Rates at 0.26 and Guidance & Credibility at 0.12 together carry 38% of the weight and both are pair-negative for the same reason: the Bank of Japan has 50-75bp still to deliver on the consensus path, with 35 of 54 economists expecting at least 1.50% by end-March 2027 and half of 36 naming 1.75% as terminal, against a Bank of England running an explicitly symmetric reaction function whose resolution it has tied to 2027 pay settlements arriving at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report and the 17 December decision — and the incoming evidence, private-sector pay at 2.8% against a target-consistent 3.25% and DMP wage expectations falling to 3.4%, leans dovish. On those paths a 275bp differential becomes 200-225bp, and the BoJ has changed its stated objective from lifting inflation to preventing an upward deviation, which mechanically converts every Japanese upside surprise into a tightening impulse. The two standalone dossiers reinforce powerfully here: sterling scored -0.4192 strategically, the weakest in its cycle set, against the yen at +0.0940, so the gap between the two legs is roughly half a point of weighted score and this is the widest fundamental spread available in the yen complex. Three bilateral considerations modify that and one of them is decisive for the size of the call. First, Factor 5 at a 0.16 weight nets to zero: Japan's +5.04%-of-GDP current account against the UK's -2.84% says short the pair on levels, while the framework's own commodity rules and Japan's faster terms-of-trade deterioration — 90.5 to 81.62 in two quarters — say own it on flow, and both energies now share one supply choke point. Third, bilateral trade at roughly USD 18bn two-way is immaterial and creates no offsetting flow. What is not priced anywhere we can find is the interaction — a BoJ terminal above 1.75% arriving in the same window as a UK Budget whose fiscal arithmetic the gilt market has already marked at 184bp over Bunds. The path of least resistance is lower in three legs: September policy compression, the 28 October to 5 November cluster where the UK Budget, the BoJ Outlook Report and the BoE MPR fall inside nine days, and a November-December resolution of the BoE's symmetric function that the wage data suggests lands dovish. base_case.path: Event-driven, saw-toothed decline in two front-loaded windows — mid-September policy compression and the late-October/early-November fiscal-and-BoJ-Outlook cluster — settling into the 201.94-203.45 zone

strategic.path_expectation: We expect an event-driven, saw-toothed decline in two front-loaded windows rather than a continuous trend, and a genuine risk of a round trip between them. Window one is 15-18 September, where the compression of the differential should take the pair through the 209.42-210.07 triangle base and into the air pocket, with the low 205s a realistic first stop because there is no qualifying zone between 208.35 and 203.45 to arrest it. Between the windows expect a grind with failed rallies back toward the broken 210.66-211.95 band and possibly the 213.04 200-day, retested from below — that retest is the highest-quality entry the horizon offers. Window two is the fortnight around 28 October to 5 November, where the UK Budget, the BoJ Outlook Report and the BoE Monetary Policy Report fall inside nine days and where a 200-300 pip risk-premium repricing takes the pair into the 201.94-203.45 zone. The shape is a stepped L rather than a V, because the terms-of-trade and fiscal drags on sterling are structural and the heating season falls inside the window, and because the 200-week average at 191.80667 is 9.86% below spot and rising only 0.281646 per week — it will not be reached, so nothing in the base case threatens the multi-year uptrend and there is no structural magnet pulling the pair further than the zones themselves. Realised volatility should rise from 8.75% toward 10-12% and stay there, since a market pricing an estimated 7.791% at 185.7 days is not pricing the calendar it faces. The largest pullback risk is a 5 November BoE hike, worth 200-300 pips of squeeze on our reading.

The pair closes below 199.51 — the top of the four-touch densest support band — for two consecutive weeks with the BoJ terminal above 2.00% on OIS and GBP net spec beyond -70,000 contracts

consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Bearish, central expectations 205.00 at three months and 202.50 at six months
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: 292 pips below the interpolated one-month path (211.42), 429 pips below at three months (209.29), and 580 pips below at six months (208.30), while remaining above the most bearish published forecast house range of 192-198
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: We differ for three reasons. Consensus underweights the September sequencing: commentary treats the 28 October Budget as the sterling event and has not marked the mechanical 25bp of compression available when the BoE holds on 17 September and the BoJ hikes on 18 September, which is why we expect the move to start earlier. Consensus underweights the BoJ terminal: pricing implies only about 1.21% after 18 December, one hike for the whole of 2026, against a Board that has written that the pace will be faster than market expectations — and the market has only just begun to reprice this. And consensus overweights the carry as a level rather than a derivative: at 275bp against 8.07% realised volatility a long looks well compensated, but that compensation is scheduled to shrink at six dated decisions inside the window, and on the payload's own arithmetic a long position has already returned approximately nothing over six months.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The edge is front-loaded, worth 173 pips against the one-month forward and 424 against the three-month, and captured inside three months it costs only 71bp of carry against 141bp at six
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: Two failure modes. The clean one is that the September decisions land symmetrically, the risk regime persists, and a 275bp carry cross simply keeps paying — the position bleeds 283bp annualised while the fundamentals slowly close, which is the modal way to lose money here and costs roughly 300 pips over six months even if spot is unchanged. The sharper one is a fourth hawkish BoE vote on 5 November or a durable Hormuz reopening at roughly 20% probability, either of which restores the differential story with the pair only 4.2% below its 52-week high and no dense resistance overhead until 219.65.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons are aligned in direction and the thesis strengthens with time, from a tactical -0.1799 at conviction 2 to a strategic -0.3594 at conviction 3, with overall confidence rising from 55% to 61%. The composition changes more than the sign. Tactically 71% of the bearish case sits in two factors and is offset by a gross +0.1393 from Risk Appetite, USD Liquidity and the commodity netting in External Balance — three descriptions of one thing, a benign and cheaply funded carry regime. Strategically six factors are negative and only one positive, because the framework reallocates weight into Guidance and Fiscal exactly where the divergence between a directional BoJ and a symmetric BoE and between two unequally credible fiscal positions lives, while the two tactical positives decay: risk appetite loses informational content once the dominant risk becomes the 28 October Budget, and the commodity netting that helps the pair tactically is cancelled by Japan's vastly better external level over six months.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Run the tactical expression in spot with a 338-pip stop at 0.63× NAV per 1% of risk, entered on a retest of the 210.66-211.95 band or on a confirmed break of 209.42, and hold the strategic view through OTC optionality at the 94.7-day and 185.7-day tenors rather than rolling spot for six months, checking any dealer quote against the store's 7.419% and 7.791% as floors rather than levels.

catalysts.rationale: The cleanest near-term test of whether the Japanese super-long sell-off is a policy repricing or a fiscal risk premium. The 28 August 2-year auction drew a bid-to-cover of 2.97 against a 12-month average of 3.74 and 25s30s is already inverted at -1.0bp. A weak tail would confirm the fiscal channel and be yen-negative and therefore pair-POSITIVE despite higher Japanese yields; a firm auction lets the policy channel dominate and is pair-negative. Reporting indicated JGB yields eased following a solid sale of 30-year debt, consistent with the pair's 3 September collapse.

July payrolls printed -23,000 with 103,000 of downward revisions and average hourly earnings at 3.2%. A second negative print questions the Fed path, and for a cross with no dollar leg the transmission is the carry regime rather than the differential: a hard-landing repricing lifts volatility and undermines a 275bp carry position, which is pair-negative. A strong rebound sustains the low-volatility melt-up that has funded the pair all year.

catalysts.event: Japan revised Q2 GDP and July balance of payments
catalysts.rationale: The GDP revision is skewed upward by a Ministry of Finance corporate survey showing Q2 capital spending at +1.6% year-on-year against a 0.2% consensus with pre-tax profits up 24.6%, which removes the growth objection to further BoJ tightening. The same release carries the July current account after June produced Japan's first monthly deficit in seventeen months — a second consecutive deficit would be pair-positive, so the release is genuinely two-sided even though the policy read dominates.

The release that most directly determines whether the BoE's hawkish tail survives, and therefore whether sterling's 275bp advantage is defended or allowed to erode. Prior prints were unemployment 4.9%, regular pay 3.5% overall but only 2.8% in the private sector, with payrolled employees down 210,000 on the year. Further loosening removes the second-round-effects case that keeps three MPC members voting to hike two days later, compressing the differential from the sterling side without the BoJ having to do anything.

catalysts.event: UK August CPI, core and services CPI; FOMC decision with projections
catalysts.rationale: The UK print is genuinely two-sided for the pair: an energy-driven upside surprise raises BoE hike odds, which is pair-positive through the rate channel, while simultaneously cutting real income and worsening the terms of trade, which is pair-negative. The FOMC matters to the cross only indirectly, through the risk and funding regime that determines whether a 275bp carry trade stays comfortable, since neither leg is the dollar. A hot UK CPI into a Fed hike is the pair-positive combination.

catalysts.event: Bank of England MPC decision and minutes with the annual gilt-reduction vote; Japan national CPI for August
catalysts.rationale: The densest bilateral day before the BoJ. The rate outcome is discounted at about +7bp, so the sterling information is in the vote split — a move from 6-3 to 7-2 thins the hawkish tail that supports the carry premium — and in the QT pace, where a slowdown would be gilt-supportive and modestly sterling-supportive. On the same day Japanese national CPI lands with the BoJ's own ex-special-factors measure at 2.3% and government energy subsidies suppressing the headline by roughly 40-50bp, so a core print at or above 2.0% would make the next day's hike a certainty. The two prints push the differential the same way.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest single event in the tactical window and the one that mechanically closes the differential from 275bp to 250bp if delivered, one day after the BoE has held. Roughly 80-90% of a 25bp move to 1.25% is priced and Takata already dissented for that level in July, so the trade is not the decision but the press conference: whether Ueda repeats the Summary of Opinions formulation that the pace will be faster than market expectations. Cumulative pricing implies only about 1.21% after 18 December, so acceleration language reprices the whole path rather than one meeting.

catalysts.event: Japanese interim fiscal half-year close and US FY2027 appropriations deadline
catalysts.rationale: Two coincident events that push the pair the same way. The Japanese interim book-closing generates documented repatriation and dividend-related yen flows, amplified this year because life-insurer hedge ratios are at historic lows so a higher share of any repatriation hits spot rather than rolling off existing forwards. Separately a US shutdown is precedented, with two already in 2026, and would be risk-negative — which in a 275bp carry cross transmits directly through the funding leg rather than the dollar.

catalysts.event: UK Autumn Budget with OBR economic and fiscal forecast
catalysts.rationale: The most consequential dated sterling event of the horizon and the mechanism by which a gilt-Bund premium of about 184bp — the widest since the 2022 mini-Budget — converts into a currency move. Chancellor Healey must satisfy fiscal rules whose March headroom of GBP 9.9bn a 39bp year-on-year rise in the 10-year has plausibly consumed at roughly GBP 2.5bn of debt service per 0.25 points. For the pair the transmission is doubled: sterling weakness on the fiscal channel coincides with the yen being the natural recipient of any risk-premium repricing, and it falls two days before the BoJ's Outlook Report.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan decision with quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: A full projection round, which moves a pair materially harder than a bare statement. The July Outlook already revised FY2027 core CPI UP to 2.4% and called CPI risks skewed to the upside; the October revision incorporates the energy-subsidy unwind and a yen weaker than the corporate planning rate. Falling two days after the UK Budget and six days before the BoE's Monetary Policy Report, it is the pivot of the strategic window: Japan frames the comparison before sterling gets to reply.

catalysts.event: Bank of England MPC decision with Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The first full BoE forecast round after the Budget and the meeting at which the three standing hawks vote again with early 2027 pay-settlement evidence arriving. This is the pair's largest single reversal risk: a hike to 4.00% would restore the differential toward 300bp against a BoJ still at 1.25%, which is the cleanest way for the bearish thesis to be wrong. The base dossier assesses a November hike at roughly 25%, and the MPR conditions its forecasts on market-implied rates, so its published inflation path is an implicit verdict on the market's 2027 timing.

The meeting at which the Committee expects to have learned about 2027 pay settlements, the input its own July minutes name as decisive for a genuinely symmetric reaction function. If private-sector regular pay is still near 2.8% and unemployment above 5.0%, the dovish resolution arrives here and sterling's 275bp advantage becomes a shrinking rather than a defended asset. It falls one day before the BoJ, so once again Japan has the last word in the window.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The single largest identified gap between guidance and pricing in either dossier. Market pricing implies only about 1.21% after this meeting — one hike for the whole of 2026 — while half of 36 surveyed economists name 1.75% as terminal and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027. A December move would be a repricing of the path rather than a confirmation of it, and it lands the day after the BoE, giving the pair two differential-relevant decisions in 48 hours for the second time in the window.

invalidators.mechanism: The pair would have reclaimed both qualifying resistance zones and the 200-day in a single sequence, which for this specific cross means the market has read the 17-18 September decision pair as differential-neutral and the 2-3 September intervention scare as an episode rather than a regime, restoring the 275bp carry as the dominant driver with no dense resistance overhead until 219.65

invalidators.condition: The pair fails to close below 209.42 — the 3 August low and triangle base — within ten trading sessions of the 18 September BoJ decision while the BoJ has delivered a hike
invalidators.mechanism: The pair-specific test is whether differential compression actually transmits to spot; a delivered 25bp narrowing to 250bp that leaves the base intact would demonstrate that the carry bid absorbs policy convergence in this cross the way it absorbed a record intervention in August, invalidating the transmission assumption underlying Factors 1, 2 and 6
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Daily close versus 209.42 with the BoJ policy rate

invalidators.condition: The gilt-Bund 10-year spread narrows below 150bp from approximately 184bp while the 10-year JGB simultaneously falls below 2.70%
invalidators.mechanism: This reverses the Factor 8 netting for this pair specifically: the UK fiscal premium the currency has not yet paid would be withdrawn by the gilt market at the same moment the Japanese long end stops repricing, restoring a widening rather than compressing differential and removing the credibility asymmetry that gives the strategic score its Fiscal contribution

invalidators.condition: UK front-month NBP gas falls below 110 pence per therm for ten consecutive sessions on a durable Strait of Hormuz reopening while Brent falls below USD 80
invalidators.mechanism: The commodity netting in Factor 5 runs pair-positive on a shock and pair-negative on relief, but a genuine reopening is not a symmetric reversal: it removes the UK's income transfer while Bank Rate stays at 3.75%, the most sterling-positive combination available, and simultaneously relieves Japan's terms of trade — the pair-level effect is dominated by the sterling rate channel rather than the commodity netting
invalidators.monitor_indicator: ICE UK NBP front-month and Brent front-month

invalidators.condition: The Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4.00% at the 5 November Monetary Policy Report while the BoJ remains at 1.25%
invalidators.mechanism: The differential would widen from 250bp back to 275bp against a Japanese path the market has only partly discounted, inverting the compression mechanism that supplies 0.1560 of the strategic score at a 0.26 weight, and it would arrive with the pair likely below its 200-day, where a reversal has 300-500 pips of unmapped space back to the 215.05-216.01 moving-average shelf
invalidators.monitor_indicator: SONIA/OIS cumulative probability of a hike by 5 November

invalidators.condition: The 30-year JGB breaks above 4.50% while GBP/JPY simultaneously rises above 213.00
invalidators.mechanism: That specific combination proves Japanese yields are rising on fiscal risk premium rather than policy expectation — in a policy-driven repricing the yen strengthens as yields rise — and it would mean the December FY2027 draft budget is being pre-traded as a yen-negative event, the one pair-positive fiscal outcome available, neutralising both the Factor 1 and Factor 8 contributions at once
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF 30-year compound yield paired with the GBP/JPY daily close

invalidators.condition: Japanese leveraged-fund net yen positioning covers to less short than -40,000 contracts while GBP/JPY holds above 210.66
invalidators.mechanism: For this cross the pair-negative flow thesis depends on a fast-money long that has to be liquidated; if the yen leg covers without the pair falling, the liquidation has already happened without producing the move, and the structural repatriation and hedge-ratio channels in Factor 4 would have to carry the strategic case alone at a 0.06 weight

assumptions: Price payload, quoted verbatim: dataPoints 130, dateRange 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03, spot 210.72084 at spotDate 2026-09-03, computationRange 2007-12-24 to 2026-09-03 (4879 weekday bars). Moving averages, zones and 200-week figures are computed over the whole stored history, not the 130 visible bars. Data-quality flags reproduced verbatim: only 2 resistance / 13 support zones met the 2-touch threshold, and 130 daily bars passed downstream represent the 1-6 month strategic horizon.

Spot-date gap disclosed: the instructed valuation date is 2026-09-01 and both currency dossiers are dated 2026-09-01, but the price payload's spot is dated 2026-09-03 — a two-session gap in which the pair fell 580 pips. Every level, target, pip calculation and distance-to-average is anchored to 210.72084 at 2026-09-03; no fresher web quote was substituted and the fundamental readings were not re-derived from price.

Direction verdict carried verbatim: all ten factor stances, confidences, evidence types, weights, weighted contributions, net scores, convictions, rationales, G10 rankings, catalysts and cross-horizon consistency text are reproduced unchanged from a first pass scored without the price payload. The price data corroborates the settled direction and argues for size/stop calibration rather than sign change.

Implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote: GBP/JPY has no listed option, so the payload's implied volatility is derived from the GBP and JPY legs through the variance identity fed a realised correlation of 0.44. The store documents the method understating true volatility by a median 14.4% across seventeen pairs and by 8.7-17.8% against direct Eurex quotes; a bias-corrected 3-month working level of 8.4-8.7% is used throughout.

Funding premium is not a rate differential: the store's -282.9bp annualised premium equals the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis by covered interest parity, and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve, so the 7.9bp wedge against the 275bp policy differential is attributed to basis. Forward points and outrights are derived on an actual/365 basis because no dealer forward quotes were obtainable.

Sovereign yield differential is stale: the payload's 212.6bp 10-year differential is built from two monthly observations both dated 2026-06-01, roughly 94 days old at spotDate and outside both freshness windows. Live prints imply roughly 216bp and are quoted with their own dates attached; the two vintages are never paired inside a single spread calculation.

Weight adjustments: four factors were adjusted from default, each within the ±0.05 limit, with both horizons summing to exactly 1.00 (Factor 1 strategic, Factor 3 tactical, Factor 8 both horizons, Factor 10 both horizons).

Bilateral trade is asymmetrically reported and immaterial: IMF DOTS 2024 shows differing partner-country reporting bases for UK-Japan goods trade; the supplied figures are used as given, and on either basis roughly USD 18bn of two-way goods trade is a rounding error against this cross's turnover, so Factor 5 reduces to a commodity-netting exercise.

Documented gaps: the pair's own 25-delta risk reversal could not be sourced from any free provider and USD/JPY/EUR/JPY proxies are used instead; no primary bank desk forecast for GBP/JPY exists in the free stack, so the consensus benchmark is an aggregator plus a cross-derivation from GBP/USD and USD/JPY desk surveys, flagged as such; quoted cross-currency basis levels for both legs are unavailable, so the implied pair basis of roughly -7.9bp is a derivation.

Inherited flags: the GBP dossier flags UK sovereign ratings as best available with Moody's variously reported and no confirmable outlook, and records collection failures for the UK 2-year gilt, the BoE sterling ERI and UK CDS. The JPY dossier flags its 160.115 USD/JPY anchor as an uncorroborated store close, September FOMC pricing as uncited, and its IMF debt/deficit figures and Japanese sovereign ratings as uncited. No stance or level rests on a flagged input alone.

Data source discipline: spot, performance, 52-week range and percentiles, all moving averages including the 200-week and its slope, realised volatility, ATR(14), support and resistance zones with touch counts, and the recent price-action narrative come exclusively from the price payload. Web search was used only for pair-specific bank/house forecasts, named chart patterns, intervention and official-flow reporting, and bilateral portfolio-flow data.
